case_title: Munna Lal v. The State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: long-standing quarrel of about ten years between the victim and the accused's side, including a property dispute
weapon: Gun (bandook), kanta (sharp-edged weapon), tamancha (locally made gun), lathi (stick); none seized
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-2, PW-3); medical (PW-1 post-mortem); recovery (bullet recovered at inquest by PW-4)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and life sentence upheld
neutral_facts: On a September morning in 1985, at about 10.00 hours, the victim and his son had come to a field after ploughing their land when four men emerged from a neighbouring field. The son stated that the men were armed with a gun, a locally made gun, a sharp-edged weapon and a stick, were hurling abuses and calling for the victim to be killed. He stated that one accused fired gunshots at the victim, another struck him with a sharp-edged weapon, another struck him with a stick, and the others beat him. A passer-by who was said to have witnessed the incident gave a similar account. Other persons said to have been present were not examined. The victim died at the scene. The post-mortem found gunshot entry and exit wounds to the abdomen and thigh, lacerations to the face and an incised wound to the abdomen. A written complaint was lodged at about 12.10 hours. During inquest a bullet was recovered from blood at the victim's hip. The weapons were not seized and no ballistic report was obtained. The investigating officer did not give evidence. A statement from the passer-by was recorded about 24 days after the incident. The families had a dispute over land and property and a long-standing enmity dating back about ten years.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock and haemorrhage; gunshot entry and exit wounds to abdomen and thigh, lacerations to face, incised wound to abdomen
motive: alleged: long-standing enmity and property dispute between the victim's family and the accused; the Court accepted the enmity as a reason PW-2 might have falsely implicated the accused
key_evidence_accepted: Medical evidence of PW-1 on cause of death and injuries; PW-2 and PW-3 testimony was not accepted as unimpeachable and was treated with caution rather than relied on alone
witness_credibility: PW-2 (son of victim) inimical to accused, testimony to be taken with caution; PW-3 a chance witness whose presence was not justified and who was not wholly reliable; PW-4's bullet recovery held doubtful
custody_duration: Served sentences in excess of 11 years and 11 months, per the judgment
bail_history: Accused were on bail during High Court appeal; directed to surrender after dismissal of appeal; later taken into custody and applied for bail
trial_duration: offence: 5 September 1985; trial judgment: 29 January 1986; High Court: 9 July 2014; Supreme Court: 24 January 2023
legal_representation: Accused: Mr. Mukesh K. Giri; State: Mr. Sanjay Kumar Tyagi
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial held
procedural_irregularity: Investigating Officer and other named witnesses not examined; weapons not seized; no ballistic report; s.161 statement of PW-3 recorded about 24 days after incident
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld. Supreme Court: appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside, accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: Courts below scrutinised evidence meticulously; PW-2 and PW-3 reliable eyewitnesses; omission to seize weapons and absence of ballistic report not fatal where credible ocular evidence exists
defence_argument: Long-standing enmity and false implication; PW-3 a chance witness whose presence was unexplained (Jarnail Singh relied on); s.161 statement delayed 24 days; non-examination of Investigating Officer and witnesses fatal; licensed gun not seized and no ballistic report
legal_principle_applied: Evidence weighed not counted; oral testimony classed as wholly reliable, wholly unreliable, or neither (requiring corroboration); defective investigation not always fatal; non-examination of IO fatal only if prejudice; benefit of doubt where prosecution story uncertain
precedent_relied_upon: Jarnail Singh v. State of Punjab (2009) 9 SCC 719 : [2009] 13 SCR 774 (referred to; defence relied on it for chance-witness scrutiny)
other_sentence_order: Appellants to be set free immediately if not wanted in any other case
